title: BEmOC and CEmOC
body:
## What it is
Emergency obstetric and newborn care is organized into two levels. BEmOC (Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care) covers life-saving services that a well-equipped health center can provide. CEmOC (Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care) includes everything in BEmOC plus surgery and blood transfusion at a hospital.

## Must-know facts
BEmOC signal functions (general list; verify the current version):
- Give parenteral antibiotics
- Give a parenteral uterotonic (oxytocin) drug
- Give a parenteral anticonvulsant (magnesium sulfate) for pre-eclampsia or eclampsia
- Manual removal of the placenta
- Removal of retained products of conception
- Assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps)
- Basic newborn resuscitation

CEmOC adds:
- Cesarean section
- Blood transfusion
- (Care for sick and low-birth-weight newborns is also expected at CEmOC level.)

- A BEmOC facility needs trained staff available around the clock and a referral link to a CEmOC facility.
- Network planning standard commonly cited: for every 500,000 population, about four BEmOC facilities and one CEmOC facility.
- Common causes of maternal death worldwide: hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis, obstructed labor, unsafe abortion. These explain the signal functions.
- Match each cause to its function: bleeding = uterotonic, manual removal, removal of retained products, transfusion; eclampsia = magnesium sulfate; infection = antibiotics; obstructed labor = assisted delivery or cesarean; baby not breathing = newborn resuscitation.
- Three delays that kill: delay in deciding to seek care, delay reaching the facility, delay in receiving care at the facility.
- Magnesium sulfate watch points (from the obstetric notes): check respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output before each dose; the antidote is calcium gluconate.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Recognize the emergency early (heavy bleeding, convulsions, fever, prolonged labor).
2. Start stabilizing measures within scope: call for help, position, IV access, oxygen, give the ordered or protocol-based drug. For a convulsing woman, protect the airway and prevent injury first, then the drug.
3. Refer with a clear message, and send the client with a trained escort if possible.
4. Communicate with the receiving facility so they prepare.
5. Document and follow up.

## Key terms and steps
- Network of facilities: the barangay health station, rural health unit, BEmOC facility and CEmOC hospital form a referral chain.
- Signal function: a key life-saving service used to classify a facility as BEmOC or CEmOC.
- Two-way referral: the client is sent up for emergency care and referred back for follow-up.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which service belongs to CEmOC but not BEmOC?" The answer is surgery and blood transfusion.
- Trap: magnesium sulfate for seizures belongs to basic care.
- Trap: manual removal of the placenta is a basic function, so a health center with a trained provider performs it.
- Trap: assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum) is basic; cesarean is comprehensive.

## Memory aid
CEmOC = BEmOC + Cut (cesarean) + Blood. This is my own aid.

## Related topics
[[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Department of Health (DOH) Concepts and Functions|DOH]], [[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]], [[Levels of Health Care and the Referral System]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]

## Check against your textbook
- Current signal function list and the standards for facilities (verify local policy).
- The handout set had no BEmOC or CEmOC material; the list and the 4:1 facility ratio come from standard emergency obstetric care teaching.
- Whether newborn resuscitation and special newborn care sit in BEmOC or CEmOC in your textbook.

title: Newborn Screening
body:
## What it is
Newborn screening (NBS) is a blood test done on the newborn to detect certain treatable inherited metabolic and endocrine disorders before symptoms appear, so treatment can prevent disability or death. In the Philippines it is backed by the Newborn Screening Act (commonly cited as RA 9288; verify). It is one of the child-health programs under the family health services.

## Must-know facts
- A few drops of blood from a heel prick are collected on special filter paper and dried.
- Timing: the maternal health handout says between 48 hours and 2 weeks after birth; other teaching says after 24 hours of life, ideally 48 to 72 hours, once the baby has fed for some time. Testing too early can miss disorders. Special rules apply to babies who are preterm or sick.
- Core disorders usually listed: congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia, phenylketonuria, and G6PD deficiency (maple syrup urine disease is often added). The program has expanded the panel; verify the current list.
- What each does if missed: congenital hypothyroidism (low thyroid hormone) causes intellectual disability and poor growth; phenylketonuria (cannot process phenylalanine) causes brain damage; galactosemia (cannot process milk sugar) causes liver damage and sepsis risk; congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes salt loss and life-threatening crisis; G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis when triggered by certain foods (fava beans), mothballs and drugs.
- Screening is NOT a diagnosis. A positive screen needs a confirmatory test and prompt treatment.
- Untreated, these disorders may cause intellectual disability, growth problems or death.
- Parents have a right to be informed; refusal requires documentation per policy.
- Newborn hearing screening is a separate program (commonly RA 9709); verify.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Explain the test to parents and get consent/documentation.
2. Collect the sample at the correct time using the correct site (the side of the heel), after warming the foot.
3. Fill in the card completely and let the blood dry on a flat surface, away from heat, sunlight and contact.
4. Send the sample to the screening center promptly (do not stack wet cards).
5. Trace babies with positive or unclear results quickly, because early treatment matters.
6. Teach parents to follow up for results.

## Key terms and steps
- Why the heel: it is easy to reach with minimal harm if the correct lateral area is used.
- Do not squeeze the heel repeatedly; do not layer blood or smear; fill each circle completely from one side; do not touch the paper.
- Birth registration and the newborn screening card are both taught at postpartum visits.

## Community and family teaching
Explain that a normal-looking baby can still have a disorder, that the test is important even if there is no family history, and that parents should ask for the result. If the result is positive, bring the baby back at once for confirmation and start treatment on schedule.

## How the exam asks about it
- Timing, specimen handling errors and the meaning of a positive screen.
- Trap: a positive screen is not a diagnosis. Collecting too early can miss disorders, and collecting too late delays treatment, so use the correct window.
- Trap: a filled-in but wet, smeared or contaminated card is rejected and the test is repeated.
- Which disorder matches which consequence (hypothyroidism = intellectual disability).

## Related topics
[[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Maternal Health Program: Prenatal Visits, Supplements and Postpartum Care]], [[Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation]]

## Check against your textbook
- The exact window (the handout says 48 hours to 2 weeks), the number of disorders in the current panel and what happens to babies born at home (verify local policy).
- The cause-and-effect list above is general medical teaching, not taken from the handout.
- Hearing screening law number and its inclusion in this note's scope.

title: VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children
body:
## What it is
VAWC means Violence Against Women and their Children. The Philippine law is commonly cited as RA 9262, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004 (verify). It covers abuse by a husband, former partner or someone with whom the woman has or had a sexual or dating relationship, or with whom she has a common child. Violence against women and children is also one of the elements of the Reproductive Health program.

## Must-know facts
- Forms of abuse: physical, sexual, psychological/emotional, and economic (controlling money, withholding support).
- Protection orders can be sought: a barangay protection order (BPO) from the barangay, and temporary and permanent protection orders from the court. Violation can be punished. A BPO is usually issued quickly and is short-lived; the court orders last longer (verify the days).
- Health workers have roles in screening, treatment, documentation and referral. Hospitals have a Women and Children Protection Unit (WCPU), and barangays are required to have a VAW desk.
- Abuse can affect children directly or through witnessing. A separate child-protection law exists (commonly cited as RA 7610; verify). Rape is covered by a separate anti-rape law, and survivor care is covered in the psychiatric notes.
- Warning signs: unexplained or repeated injuries, injuries in different stages of healing, fearful behavior, delay in seeking care, inconsistent story, injuries in places usually covered, vague complaints, a partner who will not leave her side.
- The cycle of violence is often described: tension building, acute violence, then a reconciliation or "honeymoon" phase, and then it repeats.
- Battered woman syndrome is recognized in the law as a defense in some cases.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Treat injuries and ensure immediate safety first. Life and safety come before the legal process (physiologic and safety needs before the rest).
2. Provide a private, calm, nonjudgmental setting. Believe the client; do not blame. Interview her alone, away from the partner.
3. Document objectively using the client's own words and body maps; photograph injuries if she agrees.
4. Preserve evidence if the client agrees and per protocol.
5. Refer to the Women and Children Protection Unit/desk, social worker, police and legal help.
6. Safety plan: where to go, who to call, important documents, an emergency bag, a code word with a trusted person.
7. Respect confidentiality and the client's pace of decision.

## Community and family teaching
Abuse is not the victim's fault, help is available, keep emergency numbers and a safety plan, and know where the nearest protection office is.

## How the exam asks about it
- First action with a suspected abuse victim: ensure safety and treat injuries; not confronting the abuser.
- Trap: do not pressure the client to leave or press charges immediately.
- Trap: documenting objectively means quoting the client, not writing "alleged" or your own conclusion.
- Which person issues the BPO (the barangay official) versus the court orders.

## Related topics
[[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Community Mental Health Program]], [[Rape, Rape Trauma Syndrome and Survivor Care]], [[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact law provisions, the sequence and duration of protection orders and mandatory reporting rules for health workers (verify local policy).
- The handout set had no VAWC section; the barangay and court order details, WCPU, VAW desk and battered woman syndrome come from general Philippine nursing teaching.
- Law numbers (RA 9262, RA 7610) are the commonly cited ones; verify.

title: Essential Drugs
body:
## What it is
Essential drugs are medicines that satisfy the priority health needs of most people and should be available at a price the community can afford. Philippine PHC also promotes generic medicines and tested herbal medicines as lower-cost options. In far-flung barangays, the Botika ng Barangay brings these medicines within reach.

## Must-know facts
- Generic medicines use the chemical (generic) name and are cheaper than brands with the same active ingredient. A Generics Act exists (commonly cited as RA 6675; verify). The Philippine National Drug Formulary lists essential medicines.
- The Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act (commonly cited as RA 8423; verify) supports research and use of traditional medicine.
- General guidelines for medicinal plants (handout): use the right plant for the purpose; use only the part recommended; follow the amount and directions; use only one kind of plant at a time; stop if there is any reaction; if there is no improvement after two or three doses, consult a physician; boil in enamel or clay pots, not aluminum, and clean the pot before and after; avoid plants sprayed with insecticides.
- DOH-endorsed herbal plants with their main use, scientific name and one preparation fact (handout; verify each with your textbook):
  - Lagundi (Vitex negundo): cough and asthma; boil leaves in water for about 15 minutes; divide into three parts and drink morning, noon and night.
  - Yerba buena (Mentha cordifolia): body pain; leaves boiled uncovered about 15 minutes; fresh leaves can be squeezed onto the painful part.
  - Sambong (Blumea balsamifera): swelling, diuretic, helps prevent kidney stones; boiled uncovered about 15 minutes.
  - Tsaang gubat (Ehretia microphylla): stomachache; boiled uncovered about 15 minutes; taken in two parts, one every four hours.
  - Niyog-niyogan (Quisqualis indica): roundworm (ascaris); mature dried seeds eaten two hours after supper in an age-based number; do not eat extra seeds.
  - Bayabas (Psidium guajava): cleansing wounds, mouth infections and swollen gums; wash wounds twice a day; use lukewarm solution as a mouthwash.
  - Akapulko (Cassia alata): infected skin, skin irritation, scabies and fungal skin infection; apply the juice of squeezed leaves twice a day.
  - Ulasimang bato (pansit-pansitan, Peperomia pellucida): lowers uric acid, for arthritis or gout; eaten as salad or boiled as decoction three times a day.
  - Bawang (garlic, Allium sativum): lowers cholesterol; two cloves with meals three times a day (handout).
  - Ampalaya (Momordica charantia): lowers blood sugar in mild diabetes; leaf decoction taken before meals.
- Herbal medicines complement but do not replace proven treatment for serious illness.
- Botika ng Barangay (handout): a community-run drug outlet in a far-flung, depressed barangay, run by a recognized community group or cooperative, with a licensed pharmacist who supervises, at least two trained barangay health workers as aides, and start-up funds shared by the community and local government (at least one third each).

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the client's condition, allergies, current drugs and use of herbs. Safety checks come first.
2. Refer serious or unresponsive illness; do not delay needed treatment for herbal remedies.
3. Teach correct preparation, dose and duration of the herbal remedy using verified sources.
4. Teach that herbs can interact with prescribed drugs.
5. Promote generic names and rational drug use (right drug, right dose, right time, completing courses).

## Key terms and steps
- Rational drug use: using medicine only when needed, correctly.
- Decoction: boiling plant parts; the standard preparation for many leaves.
- Barangay health worker: trained volunteer who may keep small stocks of essential medicines under supervision.

## Memory aid
Pair each plant with one organ system or symptom (cough, kidney, skin, worms, sugar, uric acid). That pairing method is the aid; the pairs above are standard teaching.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match the herb to its use, usually ampalaya, lagundi, akapulko, sambong, niyog-niyogan.
- Trap: herb safety (some parts, doses or preparations are harmful) and not substituting for treatment.
- Trap: aluminum pots and sprayed plants are wrong; one plant at a time.
- Trap: "no improvement after two or three doses" means consult a doctor, not increase the dose.

## Related topics
[[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Department of Health (DOH) Concepts and Functions|DOH]], [[Herbal Medicine: General Guidelines]], [[Common Philippine Herbal Plants and Their Uses]], [[Botika ng Barangay]]

## Check against your textbook
- The official list of herbs, plant parts used, preparation methods and amounts (verify local policy). The preparation amounts in the handout are age-based tables; confirm them before teaching them.
- Uses differ slightly between sources: akapulko is taught as antifungal (tinea) and, in the handout, for infected skin and scabies; tsaang gubat is taught for stomachache and diarrhea; the handout describes ampalaya for "mild insulin-dependent" diabetes, a wording that likely means mild type 2 (verify).
- Whether the DOH list now has more than ten endorsed plants (verify).

title: Nutrition
body:
## What it is
Nutrition is a PHC element because malnutrition (too little, too much, or the wrong nutrients) raises the risk of infection, poor growth and death in children. The national nutrition program aims to improve quality of life through better nutrition, health and productivity. Programs combine growth monitoring, supplementation, food fortification and feeding support.

## Must-know facts
Malnutrition recognition:
- Protein-energy malnutrition shows in the child's weight, height, and arm measurements compared with standards. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick screening tool. Terms: underweight (low weight for age), stunting (low height for age, long-term), wasting (low weight for height, recent severe loss).
- Marasmus: severe lack of overall energy intake. Very thin, wasted, "old man" face, hungry, no edema.
- Kwashiorkor: lack of protein with relatively more starch. Edema (often feet and face), swollen belly, thin or discolored hair, skin changes, apathy and irritability.
- Bilateral pitting edema in a child signals severe acute malnutrition, which is an urgent referral.
- Overnutrition and obesity also count as malnutrition.

Micronutrients: the three common deficiencies in the handout are vitamin A, iron and iodine.
- Vitamin A: needed for vision and immunity. Deficiency causes night blindness, then dryness of the conjunctiva and cornea (Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia) and, in severe cases, corneal damage and blindness. Children are given supplementation at set ages through a program; verify schedule and doses.
- Iron: deficiency causes anemia (pallor, fatigue); pregnant women and young children are at risk. Iron-folic acid tablets are given in pregnancy.
- Iodine: deficiency causes goiter and developmental problems; iodized salt is a main protection.
- Zinc is used with ORS for diarrhea in many programs (verify local policy).

Food fortification:
- Fortification means adding nutrients to commonly eaten foods. The Food Fortification Law (RA 8976) requires fortification of staples: rice, flour, edible oil and sugar (mandatory), while fortification of processed foods is voluntary. A separate salt iodization law exists. Fortified products may carry a program seal ("Sangkap Pinoy"). Verify the exact list and law numbers.

Program components in the handout: micronutrient supplementation, food fortification, essential maternal and child health service package, nutrition information, communication and education, home, school and community food production, food assistance, and livelihood assistance.

Infant and young child feeding messages: start breastfeeding within one hour; exclusive breastfeeding for six months (no water or other foods); add suitable complementary foods at six months (timely, adequate, safe and properly fed); continue breastfeeding to two years and beyond. The handout lists AIDS as a reason not to breastfeed; current guidance may differ.

Related laws: the Milk Code (EO 51) controlling breast milk substitutes; the Rooming-In and Breastfeeding Act (RA 7600); the Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act (RA 10028).

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Check for danger signs in the malnourished child first (poor appetite, dehydration, serious infection, severe edema): refer if present.
2. Measure weight, length/height and MUAC; plot and classify.
3. Give supplements per program schedule; feed and teach per classification.
4. Counsel on breastfeeding, complementary foods and food groups using locally affordable foods.
5. Follow up growth and household food security.

## Community and family teaching
Start complementary foods at the recommended age, give varied and fortified foods, use iodized salt, keep food clean, and bring the child for regular weighing.

## How the exam asks about it
- Differentiate marasmus vs kwashiorkor from the described child.
- Which micronutrient problem matches the sign described (night blindness = vitamin A; goiter = iodine; pallor = iron).
- Which staples must be fortified by law (rice, flour, edible oil, sugar).
- Trap: both conditions need nutrition rehabilitation under supervision; rapid refeeding is risky.
- Trap: exclusive breastfeeding means water is also withheld.

## Memory aid
Kwashiorkor = edema ("swollen"); marasmus = "wasted". My own simplification.

## Related topics
[[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Health Promotion: Concepts, Diet and Exercise|Health Promotion]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Community Mental Health Program]], [[Infant and Young Child Feeding]], [[Laws Protecting Infant Feeding and Food Fortification]], [[Maternal Health Program: Prenatal Visits, Supplements and Postpartum Care]]

## Check against your textbook
- Vitamin A, iron and zinc schedules and doses (none stated here), exact fortification list, law numbers and program names (verify local policy).
- The handout statement not to breastfeed in AIDS is older guidance; verify the current national policy.
- Definitions of stunting, wasting and underweight cut-offs (standard deviation scores) were not in the handout; verify.

title: Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services
body:
## What it is
This PHC element covers basic care of common communicable diseases (CD), noncommunicable diseases (NCD), mental health and injuries/emergencies at the community level, with referral when needed. The handout expands "T" as medical and emergency care, noncommunicable diseases and mental health.

## Must-know facts
Clinic visit standard procedures at the health center (handout order): registration (greet, family record, chief complaint, history, physical exam); waiting time (priority numbers, first come first served except emergencies); triaging (program-based cases managed by protocol, non-program cases referred to the physician, emergency cases given first aid); clinical evaluation (the nurse reaches an evidence-based diagnosis and rational treatment under DOH programs and explains the illness); laboratory exams (use a designated referral laboratory); referral (two-way system, accompany the patient in an emergency); prescription and dispensing with proper instruction; health education with one-on-one counseling.

Communicable disease treatment:
- Follow national protocols (for example for diarrhea, pneumonia, tuberculosis, malaria). Common principles: treat dehydration with oral rehydration, give antibiotics only when indicated, complete the course, and teach prevention.
- Diarrhea: assess hydration, give ORS and continue feeding; refer for severe dehydration or blood in stool. IMCI hydration plans: A (home: more fluids and continue feeding), B (some dehydration: ORS under supervision), C (severe: urgent IV or referral).

Noncommunicable diseases:
- Major NCDs: cardiovascular disease (including hypertension), diabetes, cancer and chronic lung disease.
- Shared risk factors: tobacco, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity. These are modifiable; age, sex and family history are not.
- Community roles: screening (blood pressure, blood sugar, risk assessment), lifestyle counseling, regular medication, early referral and follow-up. A package of essential NCD interventions for primary care exists (commonly PhilPEN); the local name and content: verify.
- Cancer warning signs in secondary prevention teaching (CAUTION US) and breast self-examination.
- Warning signs needing urgent care: severe chest pain, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, very high blood pressure with symptoms, very high or very low blood sugar with confusion.
- Lifestyle-related disease prevention and control is one of the five core public health programs in the Sentrong Sigla quality standards.

Emergency services in the community:
- First aid and basic life support, bleeding control (direct pressure), splinting, wound care, burn cooling with clean running water, choking relief, and safe transport.
- A functioning referral system: call ahead, send a referral note, transfer in a stable state with an escort when possible.
- Emergency hotline and ambulance availability vary: verify local numbers and policy.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Primary survey: airway, breathing, circulation, then disability/exposure. Life threats first.
2. Control bleeding and protect the neck when injury suspected.
3. Call for help or arrange transport early; do not wait for the full assessment to refer an unstable client.
4. Give first aid within scope and standing orders.
5. Document and communicate to the receiving facility.
6. Teach family prevention and follow-up.

## Key terms and steps
- Triage: sorting by urgency so the sickest get care first.
- Referral: sending to a higher level; two-way (also referring back for follow-up).
- Program-based case: a client whose problem has a DOH protocol (TB, pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria).

## Community and family teaching
Know danger signs, keep emergency contacts visible, take medicine as prescribed, do not use unproven remedies in emergencies, learn basic first aid and CPR.

## How the exam asks about it
- Priority questions: ABC beats everything; unstable before stable.
- Which NCD risk factor is modifiable? Smoking, diet, activity.
- Clinic visit: which step comes after triage? Clinical evaluation. What is done for emergency cases at triage? First aid.
- Trap: choosing a long assessment or teaching before addressing an obvious emergency.
- Trap: in the waiting line, emergency cases skip the queue.

## Related topics
[[Essential Drugs]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Nutrition]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Health Promotion: Concepts, Diet and Exercise|Health Promotion]], [[Clinic Visit Standard Procedures]], [[Levels of Health Care and the Referral System]], [[Primary vs Secondary Survey]], [[Triage Basics and Three-Level Triage]], [[Sentrong Sigla Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact treatment protocols, program names (NCD packages), hotline numbers and referral levels (verify local policy). No drug doses are given here.
- The three-plan hydration scheme is from IMCI teaching, not the handout; verify the current chart.
- Whether your textbook lists the CAUTION US signs here or under cancer nursing.

title: Water Supply and Toilet Facilities
body:
## What it is
Safe water and proper excreta disposal are the two strongest tools against diarrheal diseases, typhoid, hepatitis A, cholera and worm infections in the community. The Environmental and Occupational Health Office of the DOH sets the approved facility types, and the Sanitation Code (PD 856) is the governing law.

## Must-know facts
Water supply facilities (the classic three-level classification used in Philippine sanitation teaching):
- Level I (point source): a protected well or developed spring with an outlet but no distribution system. Serves about 15 to 25 households; the farthest user is not more than 250 meters away; yield roughly 40 to 140 liters per minute. Suited to rural areas with scattered houses.
- Level II (communal faucet or standpost): a source or reservoir, a piped network and communal faucets. Farthest house not more than 25 meters from the faucet; designed to deliver about 40 to 80 liters per person per day; about 100 households; one faucet per 4 to 6 households. Suited to clustered houses.
- Level III (waterworks system): piped connection to individual households (the handout cites the big city water utilities as examples).
- Unapproved sources: open dug wells, unimproved springs and wells that need priming.
- Disinfect a water source after it is newly built or repaired or improved. A waterworks system must supply safe, potable water in adequate quantity; new well sites need approval and compliance with sanitary requirements.
- Typical safe-source rules: a well should be protected from contamination, sited at a safe distance from toilets and animal pens (textbooks give a distance, commonly 25 meters; verify), with a sealed top and drainage away.
- Home water treatment: boiling at a rolling boil (the handout says at least 2 minutes), chlorination, filtration and storing in a clean covered container. Verify local advice for chlorine amounts.
- Water must be tested for bacteria if the source is suspect.

Toilet facilities (handout classification):
- Level I: non-water-carriage toilets (pit latrines, reed odorless earth closet) and toilets needing little water (pour-flush toilets, aqua privies).
- Level II: water-carriage toilets with a septic vault or tank for disposal.
- Level III: water-carriage toilets connected to septic tanks and/or a sewerage system leading to a treatment plant.
- A sanitary toilet prevents contact with excreta, keeps flies and animals away, prevents odor and does not contaminate water.
- Placement: away from the water source and downhill from wells where possible.
- Open defecation is unsafe.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess the source of drinking water, how it is stored and what toilets the household uses.
2. Identify the contamination risk (shared drain, nearby toilet, open container).
3. Advise the quickest safe fix: boil or chlorinate drinking water now (an immediate barrier before construction).
4. Promote construction and use of a sanitary toilet with the barangay and household.
5. Teach handwashing with soap after toilet use and before eating or feeding.
6. Report suspected waterborne disease clusters.

## Key terms and steps
- Potable: safe to drink.
- Rolling boil: continuous bubbling; time per handout is at least 2 minutes.
- Chlorination requires the right amount and contact time; do not state numbers from memory.
- Excreta-borne routes: fecal-oral spread through water, hands, flies and food.

## How the exam asks about it
- Classify a described facility as Level I, II or III. Key words: well or spring = I; communal tap = II; house connection = III.
- Choose the best toilet for a family or the best first action for unsafe water.
- Facts with numbers: 250 meters and 15 to 25 households (Level I); 25 meters and one faucet per 4 to 6 households (Level II).
- Trap: a flushing toilet near a shallow well can still contaminate the well.
- Trap: the toilet "levels" are a separate scale from the water levels, even though both use I, II, III.

## Memory aid
Level number = how close the water is to the house: I at a source, II at a shared tap, III inside the home. My own aid.

## Related topics
[[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Nutrition]], [[Environmental Sanitation]], [[Typhoid Fever]], [[Cholera]]

## Check against your textbook
- Household counts per level, safe distances, boiling times and chlorine amounts (verify local policy).
- The handout gives 2 minutes of rolling boil in its food-safety section; other books say 1 to 5 minutes or longer at altitude (verify).
- The toilet-level grouping (which types are Level I versus II) differs in some books.

title: Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws
body:
## What it is
This note groups three parts of environmental health: how waste is separated and disposed of, how food is kept safe, and the main laws that govern sanitation.

## Must-know facts
Waste:
- Segregate at source: biodegradable (food scraps, leaves), non-biodegradable/residual, recyclable, and special or hazardous waste (batteries, chemicals).
- Health-care waste is separated into infectious/pathological, sharps, chemical, pharmaceutical, radioactive and general waste. Sharps go into puncture-resistant containers; infectious waste goes into designated bags and containers.
- Color coding is used for bins and bags. The fundamentals handout lists: black = non-biodegradable, green = biodegradable, yellow = infectious, red = puncture-resistant sharps, orange = radioactive. The assignment of colors is regulated and has changed over time, so verify the current DOH health-care waste and local solid-waste color codes.
- Safe disposal methods include composting, sanitary landfill, controlled treatment (such as autoclaving) and the barangay materials recovery facility. Open burning and open dumping are discouraged.

Food sanitation:
- Food-borne illness comes from contaminated food, hands, water, pests and poor storage.
- The four "rights" of food safety (handout):
  - Right source: buy fresh food; check expiry dates; avoid dented, bulging or broken-seal cans; boil water (rolling boil at least 2 minutes).
  - Right preparation: keep raw and cooked foods apart; use pasteurized milk and juice; wash vegetables eaten raw; wash hands and utensils before and after preparing food; keep the kitchen floor clean.
  - Right cooking: cook thoroughly so all parts reach about 70 degrees Celsius; eat promptly; wash hands before and after eating.
  - Right storage: cooked food not left at room temperature more than two hours; use tightly sealed containers; if keeping longer than about 4 to 5 hours, keep hot (at or above 60 C) or cold (10 C or below per the handout); do not overload the refrigerator with warm food; reheat to at least 70 C. "When in doubt, throw it out."
- Food handlers need regular health examinations/certificates and should not handle food when ill with diarrhea, skin infection or respiratory infection. The DOH requires laboratories to examine food handlers' stools by the formalin-ether concentration technique, not the direct smear. Establishments need sanitary permits and are inspected for source, containers, transport and handler certificates.
- Food establishments are rated Class A (excellent), Class B (very satisfactory) and Class C (satisfactory).
- Control flies, cockroaches and rodents with clean storage and waste management.

Laws (commonly cited in nursing reviews; verify numbers and content):
- Code on Sanitation of the Philippines (PD 856): water, food, excreta, waste, housing and other sanitation rules.
- Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Waste Control Act (RA 6969, 1990).
- Ecological Solid Waste Management Act (RA 9003, 2000): segregation and local solid waste plans.
- Clean Water Act (RA 9275, 2004) and Clean Air Act (RA 8749, 1999): water and air quality.
- Mandatory notifiable disease reporting law (commonly RA 11332).

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Inspect and assess hazards (open dump, fly breeding, food handling, unsafe storage).
2. Protect health first: isolate or treat sick food handlers or affected persons, then remove the hazard.
3. Teach and demonstrate segregation, handwashing and safe food preparation.
4. Work with the barangay sanitary inspector and officials for enforcement.
5. Report outbreaks and keep records.

## Key terms and steps
- Sanitary inspector: the local officer who enforces sanitation rules.
- Vector: insects and rodents that carry disease; remove food, water and shelter for them.
- Health certificate: required for food handlers, cooks and helpers, renewed on schedule.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which bin or container is right for a given waste? Reason through category first, then check your color table.
- Which action is the first step to prevent food poisoning in a community? Prevention via handwashing, cooking and storage beats treatment.
- Link a law to its topic (food, solid waste, water, air, toxic waste).
- Trap: food safety numbers (70 C core, 2 hours at room temperature, 60 C hot and 10 C or lower cold per the handout).

## Related topics
[[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Department of Health (DOH) Concepts and Functions|DOH]], [[Environmental Sanitation]], [[Typhoid Fever]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
- The color code tables (the handout list is a nursing-fundamentals version, not necessarily the DOH regulation), the law numbers, the food holding temperatures and the health certificate rules (verify local policy).
- The handout's cold-holding limit of 10 C is higher than the 5 C commonly taught elsewhere; verify.
- The rating classes for food establishments and which office issues the sanitary permit.

title: Community Mental Health Program
body:
## What it is
The Mental Health Program brings basic mental health care into primary care and the community, so people can get help close to home, without stigma. The national law is commonly cited as the Mental Health Act (RA 11036, 2018; verify). Mental health is listed with medical and emergency care and noncommunicable diseases under the "T" element of PHC.

## Must-know facts
- Mental health is a part of overall health. Community care tries to prevent problems, find them early, treat and support recovery in the community instead of institutions.
- Services are integrated into primary care, with referral to specialists and hospitals for severe or complex cases.
- Rights approach: dignity, informed consent, privacy and protection against discrimination.
- Common community concerns: depression, anxiety, substance use, suicide risk, stress after disasters and violence, dementia in older adults, and mental health of adolescents.
- Warning signs of risk: talking about death or wanting to die, giving away belongings, hopelessness, withdrawal, sudden changes in behavior, substance misuse, major losses. Higher risk when there is a specific plan, available means and a past attempt.
- Stigma and myths prevent care-seeking; education reduces them.
- Barangay and community volunteers can be trained to recognize problems and refer.
- Levels of prevention in mental health (handout lists mental health rehabilitation as an example of tertiary prevention): primary = promotion, coping skills and stigma reduction; secondary = early detection and treatment; tertiary = rehabilitation and relapse prevention.
- Psychological first aid after crises and disasters is commonly taught as look, listen, link: check safety and needs, listen without forcing the person to talk, and connect to information and services.
- A crisis is a temporary state of disorganization when usual coping fails; crisis intervention is short-term, focused on safety and restoring function.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Ensure safety first: if a person is at risk of harming self or others, stay with them, remove means, and get urgent help. Safety is the first priority (Maslow safety need).
2. Build rapport and listen without judgment; ask directly about suicidal thoughts when concerned, since asking does not plant the idea.
3. Assess needs and basic functioning (sleep, eating, support).
4. Provide psychological first aid and stress reduction when a crisis or disaster has happened.
5. Refer for evaluation and treatment, arrange follow-up and involve family.
6. Teach coping skills, healthy routines and how to get help.

## Key terms and steps
- Psychological first aid: practical, supportive care that offers comfort, safety and information without forcing the person to talk.
- Primary, secondary and tertiary prevention applies: promotion and stigma reduction, early detection, then rehabilitation and relapse prevention.
- Therapeutic responses: open-ended, reflective, empathic; avoid advice-giving, false reassurance and "why" questions.

## Community and family teaching
Mental illness is treatable, it is not shameful or caused by weakness, encourage taking medicines as prescribed, keep a routine, avoid alcohol and drugs, and know crisis contacts (verify local numbers).

## How the exam asks about it
- Safety first with a person expressing suicidal thoughts, then therapeutic communication, then referral.
- Therapeutic responses: open, empathic, not false reassurance.
- Trap: arguing with or minimizing feelings; promising to keep a suicide plan secret.
- Trap: leaving a suicidal person alone to "give them privacy."
- Which level of prevention: rehabilitation of a recovering client is tertiary.

## Related topics
[[Primary Health Care Basics|Primary Health Care]], [[VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children]], [[Health Promotion: Concepts, Diet and Exercise|Health Promotion]], [[Nutrition]], [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]], [[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts]], [[Three Levels of Prevention]]

## Check against your textbook
- Program names, the current guideline for community mental health in primary care, and local hotline numbers (verify local policy).
- The handout gave almost no detail on this program; the psychological first aid steps and suicide risk factors come from general psychiatric nursing teaching.
- The Mental Health Act's number and year, and which services it assigns to the barangay and the LGU.

title: Epidemiology and Endemic Diseases
body:
## What it is
The "Locally endemic diseases" element of PHC: understanding disease patterns in the community with data, and controlling the diseases that are regularly present. This is a hub note that points to the detailed notes.

## Must-know facts
- Epidemiology and surveillance data guide which diseases to control: see [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]].
- The diseases that are regularly present in an area, with cause, spread, signs and control: see [[Locally Endemic Diseases]].
- Numbers used to describe community health: [[Vital Statistics]] and [[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]].
- Patterns of occurrence: sporadic (few scattered cases), endemic (usual constant level), epidemic (unusually many in a short time), pandemic (several countries). Handout examples of endemic areas: schistosomiasis in Leyte and Samar, filariasis in Sorsogon, malaria in Palawan.
- Control follows the epidemiologic triangle (agent, host, environment) and the chain of infection; the easiest link to break is the mode of transmission.
- Disease detail notes for the commonly endemic infections: [[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]], [[Dengue Fever]], [[Malaria]], [[Schistosomiasis]], [[Filariasis]], [[Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)]], [[Rabies]], [[Leptospirosis]].

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Treat urgent cases first, then report and investigate, because early reporting stops spread.
2. Analyze local data and target the biggest or fastest-growing problem.
3. Break the chain of transmission at the weakest link (agent, host or environment).
4. Use the levels of prevention: protect the well, find cases early, rehabilitate the affected.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the disease from vector or reservoir, choose the control that breaks transmission, or compute a rate. Trap: epidemic is judged against the expected level of that place, not by raw numbers.

## Related topics
[[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Vital Statistics]], [[Incidence, Prevalence and Population Pyramid]], [[Three Levels of Prevention]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission]], [[Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence]]

## Check against your textbook
- Which diseases your textbook treats as locally endemic (verify local policy).
- Endemic areas change as control programs succeed; the provinces named here come from one handout.

title: Environmental Sanitation
body:
## What it is
The sanitation element of PHC: making the physical environment safe through clean water, proper excreta disposal, waste management, safe food and vector control. Environmental health is the branch of public health that prevents illness by managing the environment and changing behavior to cut exposure to harmful agents. This is a hub note that points to the detailed notes.

## Must-know facts
- Water supply levels and toilet types: [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]].
- Waste segregation, food safety and the main sanitation laws: [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]].
- Poor sanitation drives diarrheal disease, typhoid, hepatitis A, worm infections and vector-borne disease, so sanitation is prevention at the primary level.
- Core laws to recognize: PD 856 (Sanitation Code), RA 6969 (toxic and hazardous waste), RA 8749 (Clean Air), RA 9003 (solid waste), RA 9275 (Clean Water).
- Core numbers to recognize: Level I water serves about 15 to 25 households; Level II has a faucet per 4 to 6 households within 25 meters; food cooked to about 70 C; cooked food not left out more than 2 hours.
- Environmental sanitation also covers housing, vector control, and the Sentrong Sigla core program on environmental health.

## What the nurse does (priority order and why)
1. Assess household water, toilet, waste and food handling.
2. Fix the highest-risk exposure first (unsafe drinking water, open defecation).
3. Teach, demonstrate and organize the community; work with the sanitary inspector.
4. Report outbreaks and follow up.

## How the exam asks about it
Classify a facility, pick the best first action, or link a law to its topic. Trap: boiling or chlorinating drinking water is the quick first fix; building a toilet is the lasting fix.

## Related topics
[[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Elements of Primary Health Care]], [[Sentrong Sigla Program]], [[Typhoid Fever]], [[Cholera]]

- Law numbers cited here come from the community health handout; verify each.
